subsection: 6. The Catholic Church, the GAA, Protestant churches and the Orange Order abroad

notes.b: Irish priests, bishops and religious sisters shaped Catholic communities overseas, and their institutions kept a sense of Irishness alive.
points: Irish-born priests and bishops were prominent in the American Catholic Church through much of the 19th century, and Irish dominance of the hierarchy lasted for decades.
Irish communities built parish churches, and many were dedicated to Irish saints such as Patrick and Brigid.
The Third Plenary Council of Baltimore in 1884 required every parish to establish a school for Catholic children, which made parochial schools central to Catholic life.
St Patrick’s Cathedral in New York was completed in 1879, and it became a symbol of the Irish-led Catholic presence in the city.
Religious orders with Irish members, including the Sisters of Mercy and the Christian Brothers, ran schools, hospitals and charitable houses in the USA, Britain and Australia.
Catholic fraternal societies such as the Ancient Order of Hibernians offered insurance, funeral benefits and social life to Irish Catholic men.

notes.b: Daniel Mannix was an Irish-born Catholic archbishop in Melbourne, whose opposition to conscription and support for Irish independence made him a controversial figure.
points: Daniel Mannix was born in Charleville, County Cork, in 1864, and he trained for the priesthood in Ireland.
He was appointed coadjutor archbishop of Melbourne in 1912, and he became archbishop in 1917.
As archbishop he opposed conscription in Australia, and he took a leading part in the campaign against it in the referendums of 1916 and 1917, which were both defeated.
He supported Irish independence and criticised British policy in Ireland, which made him a target for British loyalist opinion in Australia.
In 1920 British authorities removed him from a ship bound for Ireland, to stop him landing there.
He clashed with the Orange Order and other Protestant organisations in Victoria, and sectarian disputes shaped Melbourne politics in his time.
Contemporary attitudes were sharply divided: Irish Australians and many Catholics admired him, while nationalists and imperial loyalists in Australia called him disloyal.
Historians present him as a major figure in Australian Catholic and political life, and they debate how far his nationalism was tied to his loyalty to the Church.
He died in 1963, aged 99, after a long episcopate in Melbourne.

notes.b: The Gaelic Athletic Association was founded in Ireland in 1884, and it reached Irish communities overseas through clubs and tours.
points: The GAA was founded at Thurles, County Tipperary, in November 1884, and its founders included Michael Cusack and Maurice Davin.
The GAA promoted Gaelic football and hurling, and it also organised athletics, as a way of building a distinctly Irish sporting culture.
In 1888 a team of Irish athletes toured the United States, playing Gaelic games and athletics and drawing Irish-American crowds.
Irish-American clubs playing Gaelic football and hurling appeared in New York, Chicago, Boston and other cities with large Irish populations.
Clubs in Britain and Australia also played Gaelic games, and they gave Irish emigrants a regular social life built around their identity.
The GAA linked sport with nationalism: its rules barred members from playing foreign games, and clubs abroad were part of the same nationalist culture.

notes.b: Protestant emigrants from Ulster, often called Scotch-Irish, kept a Presbyterian and Methodist identity that was distinct from Irish Catholic nationalism.
points: Ulster Presbyterians settled in Pennsylvania and along the Appalachians in the 18th century, and their descendants in the USA became known as Scotch-Irish.
Presbyterian and Methodist congregations in the USA and Canada kept links with the churches in Ireland and recruited ministers from them.
The Ulster-Scots identity stressed Protestant descent, loyalty to the British Crown and a sense of a separate heritage from the Irish Catholic majority.
Many Protestant emigrants assimilated quickly into American and Canadian denominations, and their sense of Irishness faded more quickly than that of Catholics.
In Canada Ulster-Scots and Presbyterian identity was strong in Ontario, and it was linked to loyalty to the British connection.

notes.h: The Orange Order in Canada and Australia
notes.b: The Orange Order was founded in Ireland in 1795, and it carried a Protestant and loyalist identity to Canada and Australia, where it was politically significant.
points: The Orange Order was founded in County Armagh in 1795, after the Battle of the Diamond between Protestant and Catholic groups.
The Grand Orange Lodge of British America was formed in 1830, and it coordinated the Orange lodges across Canada.
Orange lodges in Toronto and Ontario were politically influential, and Orangemen played a major role in provincial and municipal politics.
Orange parades on 12 July, known as the Twelfth, marked the Battle of the Boyne and were occasions of public display and occasional violence in Canada.
Orange lodges were established in colonial New South Wales and Victoria in the 19th century, and they opposed Catholic influence and Home Rule.
In Australia the Orange Order was part of a loyalist and anti-Catholic culture, and it clashed with Catholic institutions in Melbourne and Sydney.

notes.h: How church, sport and community sustained Irishness
notes.b: Church, sport and community life worked together to sustain a sense of Irishness abroad, though many emigrants and their children took part in only some of them.
points: Priests and nuns acted as community leaders, and parish events such as dances, picnics and fundraising kept Irish life visible in the city.
St Patrick’s Day parades in New York date back to the 18th century, and they became a major public display of Irish identity in America.
Church schools taught Catholic children their faith and gave the second generation a grounding in parish and community life.
The second generation often moved towards American or Australian culture, and the church and GAA supported Irishness for those who wanted it.
Catholic and Orange rivalry in Canada and Australia shaped the public life of Irish communities, and sectarian tension was a constant feature.

notes.b: In Britain Irish Catholics relied on their own priests, schools and welfare societies, and their institutions grew in the cities where Irish communities were largest.
points: Irish-born priests served many of the Catholic parishes in Liverpool, Glasgow and other British cities, where they built churches and schools for poor congregations.
The Education (Scotland) Act of 1918 brought Catholic schools in Scotland into the state system, which secured their place in Scottish education.
Catholic Hibernian societies in British cities gave members welfare, burial benefits and a social life centred on the parish.
Irish nuns ran hospitals, orphanages and schools in British cities, and their work reached poor Irish districts that the state had not served well.
The Catholic community in Britain was a visible minority, and its institutions were a focus for both loyalty to the Irish cause and sectarian suspicion.

notes.h: Assessment: church, sport and identity abroad
notes.b: Judgements on the role of these institutions turn on whether they preserved Irish identity or helped emigrants to assimilate into their new societies.
points: Achievement: the Catholic Church and GAA gave Irish emigrants a community, a social life and an Irish identity that lasted for generations.
Limit: many emigrants' children assimilated, and the institutions reached only part of the emigrant population.
Contemporary view: Irish nationalists praised the church and the GAA as guardians of Irishness, while nativists and imperial loyalists regarded them as divisive.
Later view: historians argue that the Catholic Church and the GAA sustained identity but also helped Irish communities to organise and gain power in their new societies.
Protestant and Orange identity achieved political influence in Canada and Australia, but it was often a sign of loyalty to the British connection, not of Irish nationalism.
